theme: Shout for joy to God, all the earth
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 66:1-7 slowly, twice. This is the opening of one of the Psalter’s great worship psalms. The first seven verses summon all the earth to praise God and recall his works of deliverance, particularly the Exodus. It is the right psalm to anticipate the next unit of our plan.
settingTheScene: Psalm 66 is a great national psalm of thanksgiving. The first half (which we read today) calls all the earth to worship God for his mighty works. The second half (which the plan does not include here) gets more personal, recounting how the worshiper has tested God in suffering and been delivered. Today we read the public, corporate opening of the psalm. It looks back at the Exodus, which we are about to read in detail, and summons every nation to praise the God who made it happen.
observation: Verse 1: “Shout for joy to God, all the earth.” Universal call to worship.
Verses 2-4: God’s name and glory are to be celebrated by all peoples, even God’s enemies will cringe before him.
Verse 5: “Come and see what God has done: he is awesome in his deeds toward the children of man.”
Verse 6 specifically recalls the Exodus: “He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the river on foot.”
The crossing of the Red Sea and the Jordan are both alluded to, God’s redemptive acts in history.
Verse 7: “Who rules by his might forever, whose eyes keep watch on the nations, let not the rebellious exalt themselves.”
interpretation:
Psalm 66:1-7 is a call to worship grounded in God’s mighty acts of redemption. It is, in a sense, the opening anthem of the gospel of God’s deliverance.

The psalm opens by summoning the whole earth. “Shout for joy to God, all the earth.” Notice how universal the call is. This is not a private psalm for Israelites alone. It is a summons to every people, every nation, every voice on earth. Worship is meant to be global. God’s glory is not Israel’s private property; it is a flame that every nation should burn around.

Verses 2-4 connect God’s name with his glory. “Sing the glory of his name; give to him glorious praise!” The name of God is the focus of worship. Throughout the patriarchal narratives, we have seen God revealing his name in different forms, El Shaddai to Abraham, El Olam at Beersheba, the LORD at the burning bush (which we will read soon). The whole patriarchal story has been a gradual unveiling of who God is, and the appropriate response is worship of his name.

But then verse 3 has an arresting note: “Through the greatness of your power your enemies come cringing to you.” Worship is not just from the willing. Even God’s enemies eventually cringe before him. This is not the language of universalism (every soul finally saved) but of universal recognition (every knee will bow, whether in glad worship or fearful submission). The same will be expressed in Philippians 2 about Christ, “every knee should bow… and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.”

Verse 5 invites the reader to look at history. “Come and see what God has done.” This is the basic posture of biblical faith. Look at what God has done. The patriarchal story is a record of what God has done. The Exodus is what God has done. The cross is what God has done. Faith is not blind. It looks at the deeds of God in history and worships in response.

And then verse 6 specifically recalls the Exodus: “He turned the sea into dry land; they passed through the river on foot. There did we rejoice in him.” The crossing of the Red Sea, and possibly also the crossing of the Jordan into the promised land, is mentioned as the supreme example of God’s redemptive power. This is the great event that defined Israel as a nation, and it is also the great picture that the New Testament will use for baptism, for salvation, for passing through death into life.

Verse 7 closes the section with a sober reminder. “Who rules by his might forever, whose eyes keep watch on the nations, let not the rebellious exalt themselves.” God reigns. He watches. The rebellious may make a lot of noise, but they should not exalt themselves. God’s eyes are on the nations. Nothing escapes his rule. Whatever it looks like from the ground, the King is on his throne.
connection: We are about to enter the Exodus narrative in the next unit. Psalm 66 is a fitting preview. It calls every nation to praise the God who turned the sea into dry land. The redemption of Israel from Egypt was not just a national story, it was a public demonstration of God’s power that the whole world should learn from and worship in response to. The God of the Exodus is the God who still saves his people from every form of bondage.
application:
Take the psalmist’s first command: shout for joy. The Christian life is meant to be full of joy in worship. Not somber acknowledgment, not dutiful gratitude, shouting joy. If your worship has gone quiet over time, let this psalm be a prophetic correction. The God who delivered Israel from Egypt is the same God who delivered you from sin and death. He deserves more than a polite thank-you.

And take the second command: come and see. Look at what God has done. Not just in Scripture, but in your own life. Make a habit of reviewing the redemptive acts of God on your behalf. The healings, the answered prayers, the prevented disasters, the spiritual breakthroughs. Come and see. Then sing.
prayerPrompts: Come and see what God has done, and tell him what you see in his work, from creation to the cross to your own life.
Ask him to restore your joy in worship.
Pray that the nations would join in praising him.
